## Librarian or Farmer? {.stage-slide #bayes-hook}

::: {.lede-min}
Steve is very shy and withdrawn, invariably helpful but with very little interest in people or in the world of reality. A meek and tidy soul, he has a need for order and structure, and a passion for detail.
:::

<div id="prior-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="prior-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="prior-frag-2"}

::: {.slide-footer}
The description never changes; the answer does — because of a number that is not in it. That number is the base rate, and the next slide goes and counts it.
:::

## Twenty Farmers for Every Librarian {.stage-slide #bayes-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-bayes}
<div id="bayes-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-3"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bayes-frag-4"}

::: {.slide-footer}
The base rate is how common each job is, before you read a word about Steve. His description fits librarians four times better. But there are twenty times more farmers, so he is still five times more likely to be one.
:::

## Move the prior, watch the answer move {.sim-slide #bayes-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 3 · the base rate does the work
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
prior <- 1 / 21 # <-- P(librarian)
n <- 300000

lib  <- runif(n) < prior

# fits 40% of librarians, 10% of farmers
fits <- runif(n) < ifelse(lib, 0.40, 0.10)

c("P(H)" = prior, "P(H|E)" = mean(lib[fits]))
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
The evidence is identical every time — only the prior changes. `1/21` is the real ratio, one librarian for every twenty farmers; at `0.50` you get 0.80. **The description never had an opinion about how common librarians are, so the base rate has to supply it.**
:::

## Monty Hall Problem {.stage-slide #monty}

::: {.lede-min}
A car sits behind one of three doors and a goat behind each of the others. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door 3 on a goat and offers you the swap. Do you take it?
:::

The worksheet's tree diagram drawn as area: 80% would buy, 40% of those would upgrade. Counting people or splitting a unit square is one operation — again a ratio of what survived.

## Count the managers instead {.sim-slide #cond-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 3 · Bayes without the formula
:::

::: {.lede-min}
You never need the theorem if you are willing to simulate 200,000 managers and count the ones you care about.
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
n   <- 200000
buy <- runif(n) < 0.80

# upgrading depends on whether they bought
p_up <- ifelse(buy, 0.40, 0.10)
up   <- runif(n) < p_up

# keep ONLY the managers who would upgrade,
# then ask what fraction of those are buyers
round(mean(buy[up]), 4)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
`buy[up]` **is** the conditioning step — one line doing what the tree diagram does, and what the grid did to Steve. Drop the buy rate to `0.20` and the answer collapses, for exactly the reason Steve is probably a farmer.
:::
